taxi.color: white/yellow-plate H-registered private taxis and route taxis
taxi.fareNote: Route taxis charge fixed shared fares by destination; private/hotel taxis negotiate a fixed price upfront since meters are not standard.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.St. Ann's: Hilton Trinidad and Conference Centre, St. Ann's

avoid.reason: Avoid Laventille, Beetham Estate and Sea Lots — high crime; caution downtown at night

hood_desc: Trendy strip of restaurants, rum shops and nightlife along Ariapita Avenue; best for younger travelers and nightlife-focused visitors who want to walk to bars and food.
Leafy, upscale residential area near the Queen's Park Savannah and the historic Magnificent Seven mansions; suits business travelers and those wanting quiet, central lodging.
Hillside district overlooking the Savannah with the Hilton and Botanical Gardens nearby; suits business travelers, conference-goers and those wanting resort-style comfort with skyline views.
Historic inner-city area next to the Savannah with guesthouses in colonial-era homes; good for budget-conscious travelers who still want a walkable, central base.
Affluent suburban valley north of the city with malls, guesthouses and easy hillside access; suits longer-stay visitors and families wanting a quieter, greener base with taxi access into town.
lodging: Courtyard by Marriott Port of Spain

water.note: Tap water is treated but infrastructure issues persist; bottled water is recommended for visitors.

transit.pay: PTSC buses are paid in exact cash (TT$ coins) or with a PTSC smart card at City Gate; maxi-taxis (privately operated shared vans identified by route-color bands) are paid in cash directly to the driver or conductor; Water Taxi ferry tickets are bought as tokens or passes at terminal booths.
transit.hours: PTSC buses and maxi-taxis run roughly 5am-10pm with reduced late-night/route-taxi options; Water Taxi runs limited weekday commuter schedules, not late-night.
transit.note: Maxi-taxis are the most common way locals get around, identified by a colored band (e.g., yellow for Port of Spain routes); route taxis (shared private cars) supplement this along fixed routes.

ferry: Water Taxi (Port of Spain to San Fernando)
T&T Inter-Island Ferry (Port of Spain to Scarborough, Tobago)

transit.m: Maxi-taxi to City Gate terminal (~45 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; 10% is appreciated at restaurants if service charge isn't already added, and rounding up for taxis/porters is common.

food.name: Doubles
food.desc: Two soft fried barra flatbreads around curried channa, dressed with tamarind or mango chutney and fiery pepper. The national breakfast, eaten standing up.

places.name: Sauce Doubles
places.note: Local favourite praised for rich channa and a good balance of chutney and pepper.

places.name: Mitch's Doubles
places.note: Long-running roadside stand that draws a queue of office workers each morning.

places.name: Independence Square vendors
places.note: Carts along the square and George Street sell doubles from dawn; get there before 10am.

food.name: Bake and shark
food.desc: Fried shark in a puffy fried bake, then loaded by you with shadon beni sauce, garlic, tamarind, pineapple, coleslaw and pepper at the topping bar.

places.name: Richard's Bake and Shark
places.note: The most famous stall on the beach, an hour over the mountain from the city.

places.name: Sharon's Bake and Shark
places.note: Neighbouring stand with a big topping bar and a loyal following.

places.name: Maracas Bay food strip
places.note: Row of huts behind the sand; all serve bake and shark and fried kingfish.

food.name: Roti
food.desc: Curried goat, chicken, duck or channa and potato wrapped in soft dhalpuri split-pea roti, or eaten open with buss-up-shut paratha.

places.name: Dianne's Roti Shop
places.note: Known for soft dhalpuri and generous curry fillings; a city standby.

places.name: Kanhai's Roti Shop
places.note: Western Main Road institution turning out roti and buss-up-shut all day.

places.name: Patraj Roti Shop
places.note: Family roti shop on the road north, popular for goat and duck curry.

food.name: Pelau
food.desc: Chicken browned in burnt sugar then cooked down with rice, pigeon peas, coconut milk and herbs, served with coleslaw. Sunday and lime food.

places.name: The Breakfast Shed
places.note: Waterfront canteen of home cooks serving pelau, stew and provision at local prices.

places.name: Queen's Park Savannah vendors
places.note: Evening carts around the Savannah dish out pelau, corn soup and cutters.

places.name: Ariapita Avenue
places.note: Bar and food strip where late-night kitchens serve pelau to the lime crowd.

food.name: Callaloo with crab
food.desc: Dasheen leaves pureed with okra, coconut milk and blue crab into a silky green soup, the centre of the Sunday plate with stew chicken and macaroni pie.

places.name: The Breakfast Shed
places.note: Best value place in town for a full creole plate of callaloo, stew and provision.

places.name: Central Market
places.note: Wholesale market for dasheen bush, crab and seasoning; food stalls serve it cooked.

places.name: Queen's Park Savannah vendors
places.note: Cooked-food carts sell callaloo and stewed meats alongside soups.

food.name: Corn soup and cutters
food.desc: Thick split-pea and corn soup with dumplings sold from night carts, eaten with cutters such as geera pork, souse and black pudding.

places.name: Queen's Park Savannah vendors
places.note: The classic late-night soup and cutter run; busiest Friday and Saturday.

places.name: Ariapita Avenue
places.note: Carts park along the avenue to feed people leaving the bars.

places.name: The Breakfast Shed
places.note: Daytime soups and souse from the same home cooks who make the lunch plates.

food.name: Mauby, sorrel and sea moss
food.desc: Local cold drinks: bitter mauby bark, ruby sorrel spiced at Christmas, and thick sweet sea moss made from seaweed. Peanut punch is the fourth option.

places.name: Queen's Park Savannah vendors
places.note: Coolers of mauby, sorrel and sea moss beside the soup carts.

places.name: Central Market
places.note: Bottled home-made mauby and sorrel sold by the market vendors.

places.name: The Breakfast Shed
places.note: Fresh juices and mauby to go with the creole lunch plates.

food.name: Trinidad rum and Carib
food.desc: Angostura rums are made in the city, drunk as puncheon, Old Oak or aged 1919 with coconut water, and chased by ice-cold Carib or Stag lager.

places.name: Angostura distillery
places.note: Home of the bitters and rums; book the tour and tasting in advance.

places.name: Ariapita Avenue bars
places.note: The city's main lime strip, wall to wall rum bars and beer gardens.

places.name: Rum shops of St James
places.note: Neighbourhood that never sleeps; small bars pour rum and Carib until late.

landmarks: Queen's Park Savannah
This vast circular park ringed by grand colonial mansions and food stalls is the social heart of Port of Spain, famous for Carnival festivities and evening strolls.
The Magnificent Seven
A row of ornate early-20th-century mansions bordering the Savannah, showcasing eclectic architectural styles from Baroque to Moorish that draw photographers daily.
Red House (Parliament of Trinidad and Tobago)
This striking red-hued neoclassical building has housed the nation's Parliament since 1907 and stands as a powerful symbol of Trinidad's political history.
National Academy for the Performing Arts (NAPA)
A gleaming, lotus-shaped performance venue on the Savannah that has become a modern architectural icon and beloved backdrop for skyline photos.
Queen's Royal College
A distinctive German Renaissance-style clock tower building and prestigious school that anchors the northern edge of the Savannah with striking red-and-yellow brickwork.
Fort George
Perched high above the capital, this early-1800s hilltop fort offers sweeping panoramic views of the city and Gulf of Paria along with historic cannons.
Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception
This soaring Gothic Revival cathedral with twin spires has anchored downtown Port of Spain since the 1850s and remains a striking architectural centerpiece.
Maracas Bay
Just a scenic drive from the capital, this palm-fringed golden beach is Trinidad's most famous coastal escape, beloved for surfing, swimming, and bake-and-shark.
Lion House
This grand ancestral home in nearby Arouca, tied to political icon Dr. Eric Williams, is a celebrated landmark of East Indian heritage and colonial-era architecture.
Independence Square
A lively palm-lined boulevard running through downtown, lined with markets, churches, and street life that capture the everyday pulse of the capital.

train.note: Trinidad & Tobago has no passenger railway - the last trains ran in 1968. Get around by PTSC buses, privately run maxi-taxis and route (share) taxis.

bus.note: No international bus routes - this is a twin-island nation. The state operator PTSC (https://www.ptsc.co.tt/) runs express and local buses across Trinidad from City Gate in downtown Port of Spain; privately owned maxi-taxis cover most other routes.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferry - the former fast-ferry link to Güiria, Venezuela is not operating. The main service is the domestic inter-island ferry between Port of Spain and Scarborough (Tobago), about 3.5h, run by the T&T Inter-Island Transportation Company (https://www.ttitferry.com/).
